cards.name: Romance c-palatalization split
cards.teaching_frame: Hear a French word with a soft s- where you'd expect a hard c-? Try swapping in 'ch' (Italian) or 'th' (European Spanish) mentally — they're often the same root.
cards.pattern_summary: Latin c before a front vowel (e, i) split three ways across Romance: Italian [tʃ], French [s], European Spanish [θ] (Latin American Spanish [s]).
cards.description: Learning this one three-way split lets you mentally de-palatalize any Romance word back to a shared shape. The classic test word is 'hundred': cento / cent / cien(to).
cards.caveat: Not every soft c/s/th triad is this root — verify before trusting the decoder. cielo / ciel share the Latin root; English heaven does not.
cards.source_note: Cognate Bridge sound-correspondence rule cards (docs/sound-correspondence-rule-cards.md); synchronic decoder frames

examples.note: cielo / ciel / cielo — sky; English heaven is not cognate.

cards.name: Prosthetic vowel before s+consonant
cards.teaching_frame: A French or Spanish word starting with é-/es- followed by a consonant-cluster shape may correspond to an English or Italian word with st-, sp-, or sc- at the start — just strip the vowel.
cards.pattern_summary: Latin words beginning with s + consonant (st-, sp-, sc-) gained a prothetic vowel in French, Spanish, and Portuguese, but not in Italian or English.
cards.description: High-yield for beginners because it affects common nouns (school, state, space). Strip the leading é-/es- and look for the familiar s-cluster cognate.
